① The Gemara now makes an implied ruling based on our Mishnah.
② The Mishnah states that if someone finds:
Ⓐ Fruits in a vessel.
Ⓑ Or money in a purse.
③ The fruits/money are to be returned with the vessel/purse.
The Mishnah says, that the fruits are to be returned with the vessel.
When the fruits are found inside the vessel.
⑦ And the same by the money. Inside the purse.
⑧ This implies that the Mishnah holds.
⑨ Ⓐ If the fruits were outside but in front of the vessel.
Ⓑ Or the money was outside but in front of the purse.
⑩ Then the ruling would be to return the vessel/purse.
⑪ but the finder may keep the fruits/money

① The Gemara now brings another Braisa that seems to contradict the first one.

③ Ⅰ The case:

ⓑ by the side of something with a sign.

The finder must announce and return everything.
④ Ⅰ The case: The owner of the vessel came and gave a sign on the vessel.
Ⓑ but he said, the thing without a sign, outside the vessel, is not his.
Ⅱ The ruling:
Ⓐ the finder:
ⓐ must return the vessel.
ⓑ but he may keep the thing without the sign. Which was outside the vessel.
⑤ So we see, that the two Braisos seem to contradict each other regarding the object outside the vessel which has no sign.
Ⅰ Braisa number one:
The finder may keep it.
Ⅱ Braisa number two: The finder must return it.

גמרא דף כה. אמר רב זביד
① Rav Zvid answers:
② In truth, the two Braisos are not contradicting each other.
③ but rather, each Braiso is talking about a different case:
④ Ⅰ Braiso number one:
Ⓐ it is talking about finding:
ⓐ flax
ⓑ outside of a barrel.
Ⓑ if the flax had originally come from inside the barrel.
Ⓒ some flax would surely have remained inside the barrel when it fell.
Ⓓ since all of the flax was found outside the barrel.
Ⓔ it shows that the flax did not come from inside the barrel.
Ⓕ therefore:
ⓐ the barrel, with its sign, is one lost object.
ⓑ and the flax is a totally separate lost object.
Ⓖ since the barrel has a sign.
Ⓗ when the claimer gives his sign on the barrel.
Ⓘ he gets the barrel.
Ⓙ but the flax belongs to the finder.
Ⅱ Braiso number two:
Ⓐ it is talking about finding:
ⓐ a basket.
ⓑ with fruits outside of it.
Ⓑ
Ⓒ We assume that even when they are all outside.
Ⓓ They originally came from inside.
Ⓔ Therefore, the finder must return them with the basket.

① The Gemara now asks:
② There seems to be a contradiction within the Braisa.
③ The ratio of the Braisa says…
④ If someone finds scattered coins, he may keep them.

⑥ However, the end of the Braisa says that if someone finds coins stacked like towers, he must announce them.
⑦ This implies that if the coins are just overlapping each other, the finder may keep them.
⑧ So we see that the ruling regarding finding overlapped but not stacked coins seems to be a contradiction between the inference regarding it based on the beginning of the Braisa (finder may keep it)
⑨ and the inference of this ruling based on the end of the Braisa (that the finder may keep it)

lessons.expl:
·QuestionAdas Torah · Sep 18, 2017 · 47:20
① The Gemara now asks:
② If Rabbi Hanina is talking about three coins (in our Mishnah) that are not stacked like towers,
③ then the reason why the finder may keep the three coins, if they were from the same king, is because it is not considered enough a proof that the coins were found in a way of having been placed down.
④ if so, the fact that the three coins are of three different kings, Would not help either.
Because as long as the coins are not stacked like a tower then you know for sure that they were placed there.

⑦ If so, the question returns. What is the explanation of Rabbi Hanino who differentiates between the three coins being
Ⓐ from the same king?
Ⓑ or from three different kings?

lessons.title: Explained: what Rabbi Chanina meant
lessons.text: This lesson is his explanation of the step. The Hebrew words and his translation are in the previous lesson’s word sheet.
lessons.expl:
11AnswerAdas Torah · Dec 11, 2017 · 17:55
① The Gemara concludes that this is what Rabbi Hanina said:
② In our Mishnah, when it says that if someone finds three coins, one on top of the other,
③ that he must announce them.
④ That is only if the three coins are three different sizes.
⑤ but if the three coins are all the same size,
⑥ the finder may keep them.
⑦ in other words, what Rabbi Hanina meant to say is:
⑧ even if the three coins are from the same king.
⑨ they must appear as if they are from three different kings.
⑩ by all three being a different size.
